title: Trajectory Schema
strapline: Dropped from the highchair, thrown across the room, poured off the edge — the child researching how things fly and fall.
intent: Recognise trajectory as a schema — the drive to drop, throw, kick, pour and knock things through the air and watch them travel.
Understand the learning inside it: gravity, force, direction, cause and effect, and the pure physics of falling.
Reframe the repeatedly-dropped spoon and the thrown block as serious research, and give it safe outlets rather than only 'no'.
Build gross-motor power and coordination through throwing, kicking, rolling and knocking down.
Feed the vertical and horizontal lines the child keeps drawing in the air — up, down, along and off the edge.
implementation: Provide safe things to throw and drop: soft balls, beanbags, pompoms, scarves, and a drop-and-watch station from a safe height.
Set up ramps, guttering and tubes so things can roll and travel along a line, and skittles to knock down.
Name the schema warmly ('down it goes again — you're finding out how it falls').
Redirect rather than forbid — when food is dropped from the highchair, offer a basket of things that are meant to be dropped.
Keep the throwing safe with soft, light objects and clear space, and separate 'things we throw' from 'things we don't'.
key_questions: Down it goes — where did it land this time?
Can you throw the beanbag all the way to the basket?
Which rolls further down the ramp, the ball or the car?
How many skittles fell when you knocked them?
What happens if you drop it from up high?

impact.text: A child drops and throws objects on purpose and watches where they land — researching how things fall and fly.
Toddlers throw, kick and roll balls with growing power, aiming and building whole-body coordination.
A baby drops a treasure from the tray again and again, learning that letting go makes it fall — early cause and effect.
Children explore up-and-down and along lines with their whole bodies — climbing to drop, running to throw.

enhancements: A drop-station — a basket of balls and beanbags beside a safe drop from a low platform or tuff-tray edge.
Guttering, ramps and tubes for rolling things down and along.
Soft skittles and a heavier ball for the knock-down cycle.
Water play with jugs to pour off the edge and watch fall.
Target games — a bucket, a hoop, a taped square to aim beanbags into.

playing_exploring: The child follows the urge to drop, throw and pour, choosing what to send flying.
Trajectory is tested with hands, feet and whole-body force.
active_learning: Toddlers repeat the drop or throw dozens of times, watching and refining where it lands.
creating_thinking: Children predict and test — will it fall, roll or fly? — and change the throw to change the result.
